turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... things are just kind of falling apart lately. I recently finished my bachelor's, and you know, everyone says the transition to the real world is hard, but for me it's like I can't even get the bare minimum right. 

What finally made me actually come in—which, honestly, took me like three weeks to just make the phone call because I kept meaning to do it and then completely losing my train of thought—is that I just keep forgetting basic adult things. Like paying my bills. I got a massive late fee on my credit card last month, and I had the money in my checking account, I just... totally forgot the bill existed. 

And it's really starting to cost me real opportunities, which is the scary part. I'm trying to find a job right now, but I keep forgetting to return interview emails. I'll read an email from a recruiter, think to myself, "Okay, I need to reply to this when I get to my laptop," and then it just evaporates from my brain completely until a week later, and by then the company has moved on. Or I'll completely blank on showing up for appointments. Even just following through on simple errands is a disaster, like I'll leave the house to do one specific thing and come back three hours later having done absolutely nothing on my list. It's just so frustrating because I know I'm smart, I have my degree, but I can't seem to function like a normal person, and my mom keeps telling me to just buy a planner, but I have bought like five planners this year alone and... I don't know, I just really need help.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly reports forgetting to pay bills, return emails, show up for appointments, and complete simple errands.

turns.doctor_question: Were you having similar attention or forgetfulness problems when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, definitely. It's funny you ask that because my mom actually just brought over a box of my old school stuff—you know, report cards, little art projects, that kind of thing—and I was looking through it the other day. And it's like, looking back, it was so obvious even then. Like, all the way back in elementary school, my teachers were constantly writing the exact same things in the little comment section. Every single year, it was always, "She's very bright, she has so much potential," but then it would be followed by this laundry list of problems. 

They were always complaining that I was constantly losing my worksheets. Like, I would do the homework, I swear I would do it, and then it would just disappear into the abyss of my backpack. And my desk... oh my gosh, my desk was a disaster zone. It was so messy I could never find anything in there, just crumpled up papers and broken crayons and half-eaten snacks. It was so bad that sometimes the teacher would make me stay in during recess just to clean it out, which I hated, obviously. 

And it wasn't just the losing things, either. The report cards also always said that I rushed through directions. Like, I would just skim the instructions and start doing whatever I thought we were supposed to be doing, and usually I'd get it wrong because I missed some crucial step. And the talking! I was always getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just had so many thoughts in my head, and I felt like I had to get them out right that second or I'd forget them, so I'd just blurt things out in the middle of a lesson. My third-grade teacher actually moved my desk right next to hers because I wouldn't stop talking to the kids around me. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing. It's just... it felt more manageable back then, you know? Like, when the worst consequence was missing recess, it didn't feel like my life was falling apart. But now... yeah, it's always been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes rushing through directions and missing crucial steps, indicating careless mistakes and inattention to detail.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient mentions their desk was a 'disaster zone' and so messy they could never find anything, showing difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they were 'constantly losing my worksheets' and homework would disappear into their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes they were always getting in trouble for talking and wouldn't stop talking to the kids around them.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits they would 'blurt things out in the middle of a lesson' because they felt they had to get their thoughts out immediately.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have a lot of hyperactivity now, like feeling physically restless or unable to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It's actually exhausting, to be honest. It's not like I'm running around the room or climbing on things like a little kid anymore, but it's this... this intense, internal feeling. Like, if I'm in a situation where I absolutely have to sit still—like an interview, or if I'm ever in a meeting, or honestly, even just sitting in a movie theater with friends trying to watch a two-hour film—it builds up inside me. It feels like this actual physical pressure in my chest and my arms and my legs, just screaming at me that I need to move. 

I'll start shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, bouncing my heel, playing with my rings, picking at my cuticles, just... anything to let some of that energy out. If I try to force myself to sit completely still and just be perfectly calm and professional, it gets so unbearable that I honestly feel like I'm going to crawl right out of my own skin. It's like my motor is just constantly running on high, and I can't find the off switch. Even when I'm supposed to be relaxing, like watching TV on the couch, I'm usually also scrolling on my phone or knitting or doing a crossword puzzle because just sitting there doing one thing feels physically uncomfortable. It's really embarrassing, especially in interviews, because I know I probably look nervous or fidgety, but I literally just can't stop my body from needing to do *something*.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes shifting weight, bouncing their heel, playing with rings, and picking at cuticles to let energy out.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms an intense internal feeling of physical pressure and restlessness, feeling like they will 'crawl right out of my own skin' if forced to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient states they cannot just relax and watch TV, but must also scroll on their phone, knit, or do a crossword puzzle because doing just one thing is physically uncomfortable.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states it feels like their 'motor is just constantly running on high' and they cannot find the off switch.

turns.doctor_question: Do these attention and restlessness problems happen in more than one setting, like at work or school, at home, and in social situations?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, definitely everywhere. It's not like I can just leave it at home when I walk out the door, you know? It follows me literally everywhere I go. 

Um, like, at home, it's just... well, my apartment is basically a physical representation of my brain right now. I'll be in the middle of cleaning the kitchen, right? And I'll take a sponge to wipe down the counter, but then I'll notice a coffee cup that belongs in my bedroom. So I walk to my bedroom to put the cup away, and then I see that my bed isn't made, so I start making the bed, but halfway through I realize I really need to wash my sheets. So I strip the bed and carry the sheets to the laundry basket... and then three hours later, the kitchen counter is still soapy, the wet sponge is sitting on my bare mattress for some reason, and I'm sitting on the floor of the hallway trying to fix a loose thread on a rug because I completely forgot what my original task even was. It's just exhausting. 

And then socially, oh my gosh, it's so unfair to my friends. Like, we'll go out to dinner, and I really, really want to listen to what they're saying, especially if they're talking about something important, like a bad date or a family thing. But if we're at a restaurant, my brain is just... it's paying attention to literally everything else. I'm listening to the conversation at the table next to us, I'm watching the waiter drop a tray across the room, I'm bouncing my leg under the table so hard the water glasses are shaking... and then my friend will look at me waiting for a response, and I realize I haven't heard a single word they said for the last ten minutes. I have to do this awful fake nod and smile, or I have to ask them to repeat themselves, which makes me look like a terrible, self-centered friend, and I'm really not! I just can't filter out the background noise.

And obviously, like I mentioned with the job interviews and the emails, it's ruining my professional life before it even really starts. There is literally no escape from it. It doesn't matter if I'm at home completely alone, out with people I've known for years, or sitting in a high-pressure interview with a recruiter... it's like this constant buzzing in my head and my body that just never, ever stops. I used to think maybe I just needed a different environment, like maybe if I just got out of the library and studied at a coffee shop I'd focus better, but nope. It's exactly the same. It's just me. I'm the common denominator in all these places, so yeah, it definitely happens everywhere.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on chores, constantly switching from cleaning the kitchen to making the bed to doing laundry without finishing any of them.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits to not hearing a single word their friends say during conversations because their attention is elsewhere.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as background conversations and a waiter dropping a tray at a restaurant.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes being forgetful during daily chores, completely forgetting what their original task was while cleaning.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient reports bouncing their leg under the table so hard that water glasses shake.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a constant feeling of restlessness, characterized as a 'constant buzzing in my head and my body that just never, ever stops.'
